hook: The only woman ever to rule China as emperor in her own name.

pages.x: Wu Zhao entered the palace of Emperor Taizong at 14 as a junior concubine. When he died she was sent to a Buddhist nunnery, as was the custom. But his son, the new emperor Gaozong, had fallen for her, and brought her back to court.
She rose to become empress in 655, pushing aside the old empress. As Gaozong grew ill, she ran the government for him, sitting behind a screen at court and giving orders in his name.

After Gaozong died she ruled through two of her sons, then in 690 took the throne herself and founded her own Zhou dynasty. She was the only woman in Chinese history to rule as emperor in her own right.

She widened the imperial exams so that officials were picked for their ability rather than their family, and brought able men in from outside the old nobility. She cut taxes for farmers, and her armies pushed Chinese power deep into Central Asia.
A devout Buddhist, she paid for the huge Vairocana Buddha carved into the cliffs at Longmen, 17 metres tall. Some say its calm face was modelled on her own.

She set up copper boxes where anyone could drop letters denouncing officials, and used secret police to crush plots against her. Officials were so afraid that some said goodbye to their families every morning before going to court.

Forced to step down at 80 in a palace coup in 705, she died later that year. She was buried with Gaozong, and by her tomb stands a huge stone tablet with no words on it, perhaps because she wanted later ages to judge her.

Confucian historians condemned Wu Zetian for centuries because they believed a woman should never rule. Today she is seen as a strong and able ruler who held China together at the height of the Tang dynasty.
pts: The only woman to rule China as emperor
Opened government to talent through exams
Ruled China for half a century
